analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1994 federal ban on semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 1994 assault weapons ban drew 33 cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote, dying in a House Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the core of the 1994 federal law that banned the manufacture and sale of named semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines, and would have removed the tougher criminal penalty for using such a weapon in a violent crime. It was introduced two months after the ban took effect, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and sent to its Crime Subcommittee in April 1995. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms and magazine manufacturers and dealers, who could resume producing and selling the named semiautomatic rifles, shotguns, and pistols and the large-capacity ammunition feeding devices the 1994 law barred, plus gun owners who wanted to buy them.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the legal market for the semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices that the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act prohibited, by striking the ban's definitions, prohibitions, and appendix of listed weapons from federal law.
Repeals Title XI of the 1994 crime law, the title containing the assault weapons restrictions, in its entirety.

Removes the sentencing provision that imposed a stricter prison term when a semiautomatic assault weapon was used in a violent or drug-trafficking crime, reducing penalties back to those for ordinary firearms.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost in the form of renewed legal availability of military-style semiautomatic weapons and large-capacity magazines, with no offsetting replacement for the public-safety restrictions being repealed. People harmed in attacks with such weapons would have less legal protection than under the 1994 law.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weaker gun restrictions

drawbacks.text: Re-legalizes manufacture and sale of the semiautomatic assault weapons named in the 1994 law's appendix and of ammunition magazines holding more than the law's limit, undoing the restriction entirely rather than narrowing it.

Strips the enhanced criminal penalty for using a semiautomatic assault weapon in a crime of violence or drug trafficking, so a defendant convicted of a crime committed with one of these weapons would face the same penalty as with any gun.

Supporters of repeal argued at the time that the 1994 ban chiefly listed guns by name and cosmetic features and did little to reduce overall gun crime while restricting rifles and magazines common among lawful owners; the bill offered no replacement policy to address whatever gap the ban left, and no committee ever examined that tradeoff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a clean repeal with nothing in exchange: it removed the weapons ban, the magazine limit, and the enhanced criminal penalty in one stroke, and offered no alternative public-safety measure. Whatever force the critics' argument had — that the 1994 ban's effect on crime was modest — the bill did not try to improve the law, only to erase it. The concentrated benefit ran to the firearms industry; the risk ran to the public. The tradeoff was never tested, because the bill never reached a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee's Crime Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Roscoe Bartlett introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, naming Representative Steve Stockman as a co-introducer, less than two months after the 1994 assault weapons ban took effect.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on April 24, 1995, the committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Crime.
Thirty-three members cosponsored the bill, 29 Republicans and 4 Democrats, but the Crime Subcommittee never held a hearing or reported the bill out.
The action history closes with a note on March 22, 1996, pointing to H.R. 125 for further action; no chamber ever voted on H.R. 464 before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
Because the bill died, the 1994 prohibitions on semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices remained in federal law through the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People covered by the 1994 assault weapons ban kept its protections for another two years, since the repeal never advanced; firearms manufacturers and dealers did not regain the banned market during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The 1994 gun ban survived; repeal failed

for.name: Roscoe Bartlett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the repeal bill on January 11, 1995.

for.name: Steve Stockman
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer; the bill carries both lawmakers' names.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after referring it to the Subcommittee on Crime on April 24, 1995, the committee took no further action, and no hearing or markup was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Republican — 29 of the 33 cosponsors were Republicans and 4 were Democrats — but no vote was ever held, so the chamber's actual split was never tested.

industries.note: The 1994 law barred manufacture of the semiautomatic rifles, shotguns, and pistols named in its appendix; repeal would have reopened that product line. The industry's gain in this bill came directly from removing a public-safety restriction, not from a benefit that ran alongside it.
The 1994 law prohibited new large-capacity ammunition feeding devices; repeal would have restored legal production and sale of high-capacity magazines.
Dealers could legally stock and sell the banned models and magazines again, expanding inventory that the 1994 law had removed from the market.
